lead: A full adder adds three bits and gives a sum and a carry. A wide adder chains full adders and passes carries along. The real design question is how fast the carry reaches the last bit. Ripple carry hands it stage by stage. Carry look-ahead computes every carry from the a and b bits.
prereq: You need: the static CMOS gates (AND, OR, XOR) from CMOS logic styles, and binary addition with carries.

sections.h3: Half adder, full adder and the standard cell

blocks.text: A half adder adds two bits, a and b. The symbol ⊕ means exclusive OR: the result is 1 when exactly one input is 1.
S = a ⊕ b,   C = a · b
blocks.where: a and b are the input bits; S is the sum bit; C is the carry bit.

blocks.text: A full adder takes three inputs: a, b and the carry-in c from the right column.
S = a ⊕ b ⊕ c,   C = a · b + c · (a ⊕ b)
blocks.where: c is the carry into this column; S is the sum bit; C is the carry out.

blocks.text: A carry leaves when both inputs are 1 (a·b), or when exactly one is 1 and a carry came in (c·(a⊕b)).

The standard static CMOS adder cell, usually drawn as the mirror adder, uses 28 transistors. A carry gate forms C̄<sub>out</sub>, the inverted majority of a, b and c. A sum gate reuses it: S = abc + C̄<sub>out</sub>·(a + b + c). Two output inverters restore the true polarities. Because the sum gate needs C̄<sub>out</sub>, the carry is ready before the sum.

An n-bit ripple carry adder puts n full adders in a row. Bit i of a and bit i of b enter adder i, and the carry-out of adder i becomes the carry-in of adder i+1. Bit 0 is the least significant column. c0 is the carry into it, and c0 = 0 for plain addition.

Each full adder needs two gate delays to turn its carry-in into a carry-out: one AND level, then one OR level. The worst case is a carry born at bit 0 and propagated through every stage. That happens when g₀ = 1 and every later pᵢ = 1, for example a = 1111 and b = 0001.

Here t<sub>carry</sub> is when the carry-out c<sub>n</sub> settles and t<sub>sum</sub> when the top sum bit s<sub>n−1</sub> = p<sub>n−1</sub> ⊕ c<sub>n−1</sub> settles; one gate delay is a few tens of picoseconds in a modern process.

For n = 32 the top sum bit settles after 63 gate delays and the carry-out after 64. At 40 ps per gate delay the whole result needs 64 × 40 ps = 2.56 ns, longer than a 1 GHz clock period. The layout is regular, so ripple adders stay in slow timers, peripheral registers and address increments. Faster answers are in Chapter 4.2.
Subtraction reuses the adder: a − b = a + b̄ + 1, so XOR each bit of b with a subtract line and drive c<sub>0</sub> from the same line.

Carry look-ahead stops waiting for the carry to walk. Each column computes two signals from its own aᵢ and bᵢ only. Generate gᵢ = aᵢ·bᵢ is 1 when the column creates a carry. Propagate pᵢ = aᵢ⊕bᵢ is 1 when the column passes an incoming carry on.

blocks.where: cᵢ is the carry entering column i; gᵢ and pᵢ are that column's generate and propagate; cᵢ₊₁ is the carry leaving it.

blocks.text: Substituting the recurrence into itself removes every carry from the right-hand side. For four bits:

c₁ = g₀ + p₀c₀
c₂ = g₁ + p₁g₀ + p₁p₀c₀
c₃ = g₂ + p₂g₁ + p₂p₁g₀ + p₂p₁p₀c₀
c₄ = g₃ + p₃g₂ + p₃p₂g₁ + p₃p₂p₁g₀ + p₃p₂p₁p₀c₀
blocks.where: each cᵢ now depends only on the g and p of the columns below it and on c₀; no carry is computed from another carry in sequence.

blocks.text: Every carry is now a two-level AND-OR function of g, p and c0, so one block — the look-ahead carry unit, also called LCU — builds all of them at the same time. A 4-bit look-ahead adder gives all carries in about three gate delays (one for g and p, two for the widest AND-OR), against eight for ripple. Each sum then costs one more XOR: sᵢ = pᵢ ⊕ cᵢ.

For wider adders the same trick is applied to blocks. A 4-bit block has a group generate G = g₃ + p₃g₂ + p₃p₂g₁ + p₃p₂p₁g₀ and a group propagate P = p₃p₂p₁p₀. Blocks are chained with c<sub>next</sub> = G + P·c<sub>in,</sub> giving a tree of look-ahead units whose delay grows with log n instead of n. A single-level look-ahead for n bits needs AND terms of n+1 inputs, so practical blocks stop at 4 or 8 bits.

figure.caption: The 4-bit carry look-ahead adder of worked example 1. Each column forms g and p from its own bits; the look-ahead unit makes all four carries at once, and each sum is one XOR of p and its carry.

spec.aria: Four columns with g and p values, a look-ahead carry unit producing carries c0 to c3 and carry-out 1, and four sum boxes, giving 10001 equals 17.

examples.question: A 4-bit carry look-ahead adder has a = 1011 and b = 0110, with c0 = 0. Using g<sub>i</sub> = a<sub>i</sub>·b<sub>i</sub> and p<sub>i</sub> = a<sub>i</sub>⊕b<sub>i,</sub> find every g, every p, every carry, every sum bit, and the final result.
steps: Bits: a₃a₂a₁a₀ = 1011, so a₀ = 1, a₁ = 1, a₂ = 0, a₃ = 1. b₃b₂b₁b₀ = 0110, so b₀ = 0, b₁ = 1, b₂ = 1, b₃ = 0.
Generate gᵢ = aᵢbᵢ: g₀ = 1·0 = 0, g₁ = 1·1 = 1, g₂ = 0·1 = 0, g₃ = 1·0 = 0, so g₃g₂g₁g₀ = 0010.
Propagate pᵢ = aᵢ⊕bᵢ: p₀ = 1⊕0 = 1, p₁ = 1⊕1 = 0, p₂ = 0⊕1 = 1, p₃ = 1⊕0 = 1, so p₃p₂p₁p₀ = 1101.

Carries from the look-ahead equations: c₁ = g₀ + p₀c₀ = 0 + 1·0 = 0; c₂ = g₁ + p₁g₀ + p₁p₀c₀ = 1 + 0 + 0 = 1; c₃ = g₂ + p₂g₁ + p₂p₁g₀ + p₂p₁p₀c₀ = 0 + 1·1 + 0 + 0 = 1; c₄ = g₃ + p₃g₂ + p₃p₂g₁ + p₃p₂p₁g₀ + p₃p₂p₁p₀c₀ = 0 + 0 + 1·1·1 + 0 + 0 = 1. No carry waited for another.
Sums sᵢ = pᵢ ⊕ cᵢ: s₀ = 1⊕0 = 1, s₁ = 0⊕0 = 0, s₂ = 1⊕1 = 0, s₃ = 1⊕1 = 0. Result = c₄s₃s₂s₁s₀ = 10001₂ = 17. Check: 11 + 6 = 17.
examples.answer: The sum is 10001₂ = 17, with g₃g₂g₁g₀ = 0010, p₃p₂p₁p₀ = 1101 and carries c₁ = 0, c₂ = 1, c₃ = 1, c₄ = 1.
examples.check:
a=0b1011
b=0b0110
c0=0
g=[((a>>i)&1)&((b>>i)&1) for i in range(4)]
p=[((a>>i)&1)^((b>>i)&1) for i in range(4)]
c=[c0]
for i in range(4): c.append(g[i]|(p[i]&c[i]))
s=[p[i]^c[i] for i in range(4)]
print(g,p,c[1:],s,c[4]*16+s[3]*8+s[2]*4+s[1]*2+s[0])

examples.question: A 32-bit ripple carry adder uses full adder cells that turn carry-in into carry-out in 2 gate delays and form their sum one XOR delay after their carry-in arrives. Each gate delay is 40 ps. Find the worst-case delay to the top sum bit and to the carry-out.
steps: Worst case: a carry born at bit 0. g₀ is ready after 1 gate delay and c₁ after 2; each stage adds 2, so cᵢ arrives at 2i: c₃₁ at 62, c₃₂ at 64.
Top sum bit: s₃₁ = p₃₁ ⊕ c₃₁ needs one XOR after c₃₁, so it settles at 62 + 1 = 63 gate delays.
Time: s₃₁ at 63 × 40 ps = 2520 ps = 2.52 ns; c₃₂ at 64 × 40 ps = 2560 ps = 2.56 ns. The adder is finished only when both have settled.
examples.answer: The top sum bit settles at 63 gate delays (2.52 ns) and the carry-out at 64 gate delays (2.56 ns), so the adder needs 2.56 ns.

traps: Mixing the two definitions of p. Some texts use pᵢ = aᵢ + bᵢ: the carry recurrence still holds, but sᵢ = pᵢ ⊕ cᵢ is then wrong; write aᵢ ⊕ bᵢ ⊕ cᵢ. State your choice.

Timing the top sum bit from c<sub>n</sub>. The top sum bit is s<sub>n−1</sub> = p<sub>n−1</sub> ⊕ c<sub>n−1</sub>, so it settles at 2n − 1 gate delays; the carry-out c<sub>n</sub>, at 2n, is the last output to settle.
Index slip: the recurrence is cᵢ₊₁ = gᵢ + pᵢcᵢ, driven by column i, not gᵢ₊₁.
Building a single-level look-ahead for 32 bits. The AND terms grow to 33 inputs and the gate becomes huge and slow; use 4-bit blocks with group generate and group propagate.

quiz.q: Write the half-adder sum and carry equations.
quiz.a: S = a ⊕ b and C = a · b, where a and b are the input bits, S is the sum bit and C is the carry bit.

quiz.q: In a ripple carry adder, why does the carry-out settle one gate delay after the top sum bit?
quiz.a: Both wait for c<sub>n−1</sub>, which arrives at 2(n−1) gate delays. The top sum bit s<sub>n−1</sub> = p<sub>n−1</sub> ⊕ c<sub>n−1</sub> needs one XOR, so it settles at 2n − 1. The carry-out c<sub>n</sub> = g<sub>n−1</sub> + p<sub>n−1</sub>c<sub>n−1</sub> needs an AND and an OR, so it settles at 2n.

quiz.q: A column has g₀ = 0, p₀ = 1 and c₀ = 1. Find c₁.
quiz.a: c₁ = g₀ + p₀c₀ = 0 + 1·1 = 1: the column propagates the incoming carry.

quiz.q: For the 4-bit ripple adder a = 1011 and b = 0110 with c0 = 0, when is each carry ready? Compare with the worst-case bound for n = 4.
quiz.a: g₀ = 1·0 = 0; g₁ = 1·1 = 1; p₂ = 0⊕1 = 1; p₃ = 1⊕0 = 1. The carry is born at column 1, so c₂ is ready at 2 gate delays (g₁ at 1, then the OR), c₃ at 4 and c₄ at 6. The top sum bit s₃ = p₃ ⊕ c₃ settles at 5. The worst-case bounds for n = 4 are 2n = 8 for c₄ and 2n − 1 = 7 for s₃; this input finishes 2 gate delays early because no carry starts at column 0.

quiz.q: Why does a single-level look-ahead carry unit stop scaling beyond about 8 bits?
quiz.a: The equation for c<sub>n</sub> contains a product term p<sub>n−1</sub>p<sub>n−2</sub>…p₀c₀, so the widest gate needs n+1 inputs. In static CMOS a wide AND means long series stacks or a chain of gates, which adds delay, area and capacitance. Blocking with group generate and group propagate keeps every gate small and turns the delay into a logarithmic tree.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production adders use parallel prefix networks such as Kogge-Stone and Brent-Kung, which keep logarithmic depth with different area and wiring costs, and the Ling adder, which shortens the critical path. Search for "parallel prefix adder".
